overview:
Cameroon sits at the hinge of West and Central Africa, where the continent's coastline bends sharply south. It is a little larger than California and touches Nigeria, Chad, the Central African Republic, Congo, Gabon, and Equatorial Guinea. People call it Africa in miniature because almost every landscape on the continent appears here: beaches, rainforest, mountains, savanna, and near-desert. The capital, Yaoundé, spreads over seven hills inland, while Douala on the coast is the biggest city and main port.

About 28 million people live in Cameroon, speaking more than 250 languages. English and French are both official, a legacy of the country being split between British and French rule; most regions speak French, and two western regions speak English. Cameroon is a republic with a president who has held office since 1982. Farmers grow cocoa, coffee, bananas, and cotton, and oil is exported from the coast. The country is famous for soccer, for its music, and for the wildlife of its forests.
landAndNature: Mount Cameroon, an active volcano near the coast, rises 4,040 meters straight from the sea and is the highest peak in West and Central Africa; its slopes are among the rainiest places on Earth. Dense rainforest covers the south, home to forest elephants, lowland gorillas, chimpanzees, and the rare drill monkey. Dja Faunal Reserve is one of Africa's largest protected rainforests. Toward the north the forest gives way to grassy highlands and then to hot savanna, where Waza National Park has lions, giraffes, and elephants. The far north reaches Lake Chad and the edge of the Sahel. The Sanaga is the longest river. Lake Nyos in the northwest is a crater lake that released a deadly cloud of carbon dioxide in 1986.
peopleAndCulture: Cameroonians belong to many peoples, including the Bamiléké and Bamoun of the western highlands, the Fulani and Kanuri of the north, the Beti and Bassa of the south, and the Baka, forest dwellers famous for their hunting skill and complex singing. Christians live mostly in the south, Muslims in the north. Ndolé, a stew of bitter leaves, peanuts, and fish or shrimp, is the best-known dish, eaten with plantains or fufu. Makossa music from Douala and bikutsi from Yaoundé are danced across Africa. Soccer is a national obsession: the Indomitable Lions have won the Africa Cup of Nations five times and reached the World Cup quarterfinals in 1990, and Cameroon took Olympic gold in 2000.
history: Bantu-speaking farmers spread from this region across much of Africa thousands of years ago. The Sao culture built towns near Lake Chad, and later kingdoms such as Bamoun developed their own writing system. Portuguese sailors arriving in 1472 named the Wouri River Rio dos Camarões, river of shrimp, giving Cameroon its name. Germany made it a colony in 1884; after World War I it was divided between France and Britain. French Cameroon gained independence on January 1, 1960, and part of British Cameroon joined it in 1961, while the rest joined Nigeria. Ahmadou Ahidjo governed until 1982, when Paul Biya became president. Since 2017 conflict between the government and separatists in the English-speaking regions has displaced hundreds of thousands of people.
funFacts: Cameroon's name comes from the Portuguese word for shrimp, after sailors found the Wouri River teeming with them.
In 1990 Cameroon became the first African team to reach a World Cup quarterfinal, led by 38-year-old striker Roger Milla.
Debundscha, at the foot of Mount Cameroon, receives about 10 meters of rain a year, among the highest totals on Earth.
The Bamoun king Njoya invented an alphabet for his language around 1896 and later built a printing press for it.
Cameroon has more than 250 languages, one of the highest counts of any country in the world.
